steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on egocentric gaze anticipation that uses audio as well as video. Motivate the task, argue why audio helps, explain why existing audio-visual fusion falls short in the egocentric setting, introduce our CSTS model, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Egocentric gaze anticipation: motivation and difficulty
- Audio as an auxiliary cue (Fig. 1 example)
- Gaps in prior work; why simultaneous audio-visual fusion falls short
- Proposed CSTS method and evaluation
- Contributions

  - applications: AR, Wearable Computing, social scenarios; memory aids for patients w/ cognitive impairments; lower latency of content delivery in AR

  - audio-visual learning methods commonly (cite) fuse embeddings simultaneously in time and space
  - not ideal in egocentric setting: reaction to audio -> drastic viewpoint change (Fig. 1: paper -> standing person -> sitting person; head movement, first vs last frame)
  - natural delay of reaction time: stimulus and gaze reaction not at same time
  - model needs (1) viewpoint/scene change driven by audio over time, (2) locate future gaze target in visual space
  - simultaneous fusion -> spurious audio-visual correlations, limited performance; spatial-temporal separable fusion better

  - video frames -> video encoder; audio spectrograms -> audio encoder
  - spatial fusion module + temporal fusion module in parallel, self-attention; spatial and temporal correlation separately
  - branch outputs merged by channel-wise reweighting -> visual decoder -> future gaze target
  - multi-modal contrastive loss (cite) on reweighted representations = post-fusion contrastive loss; audio-visual correspondence learning
  - datasets (social scenarios, everyday activities): Ego4D (cite), Aria (cite); state-of-the-art on both

  - first approach using visual + audio signals for egocentric gaze behaviors
  - CSTS: spatio-temporal separable fusion module + post-fusion contrastive learning
  - experiments on Ego4D (cite), Aria (cite); audio +2.5% / +2.4% F1; beats prior state of the art by +1.9% / +1.6% F1

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The eye movements of a person during daily activities reflect their intentions and goals (a representative cognitive science study shows this). Because of this, being able to predict where the camera-wearer will look in the future from egocentric videos, which is called egocentric gaze anticipation, is a key step toward understanding and modeling cognitive processes and decision making. This ability could also enable new applications in Augmented Reality and Wearable Computing, especially in social scenarios, for example memory aids for patients with cognitive impairments, or reducing the latency of content delivery in such AR systems. But forecasting the gaze fixations of a camera-wearer only from the egocentric view (i.e., with no eye tracking at test time) is very challenging, because egocentric scene content is complex and gaze behavior is dynamic.

We think audio signals can be an important auxiliary cue for forecasting egocentric gaze. Look at the example in Fig. 1. In the input sequence the camera view shifts from the paper the camera wearer is holding to the standing speaker, who asks a question. Then the sitting speaker on the far right answers the question, and this is captured in the audio stream. In the anticipation sequence the camera wearer's gaze moves to the sitting person's head after hearing her response. Here the audio stream (the response of the sitting person) is an important stimulus that triggers the gaze movement. Neuroscience research also shows that audio signals influence eye movements. So we address the problem of forecasting the gaze fixation of the camera-wearer in unseen future frames, using a short egocentric video clip and the corresponding audio. As Fig. 1 shows, because the model can fuse the audio and visual cues it correctly predicts the future attention to the seated subject.

  - video frames -> video encoder; audio spectrograms -> audio encoder
  - spatial fusion module + temporal fusion module in parallel, self-attention; spatial and temporal correlation separately

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The eye movements of a person during daily activities reflect their intentions and goals (a representative cognitive science study shows this). Because of this, being able to predict where the camera-wearer will look in the future from egocentric videos, which is called egocentric gaze anticipation, is a key step toward understanding and modeling cognitive processes and decision making. This ability could also enable new applications in Augmented Reality and Wearable Computing, especially in social scenarios, for example memory aids for patients with cognitive impairments, or reducing the latency of content delivery in such AR systems. But forecasting the gaze fixations of a camera-wearer only from the egocentric view (i.e., with no eye tracking at test time) is very challenging, because egocentric scene content is complex and gaze behavior is dynamic.

We think audio signals can be an important auxiliary cue for forecasting egocentric gaze. Look at the example in Fig. 1. In the input sequence the camera view shifts from the paper the camera wearer is holding to the standing speaker, who asks a question. Then the sitting speaker on the far right answers the question, and this is captured in the audio stream. In the anticipation sequence the camera wearer's gaze moves to the sitting person's head after hearing her response. Here the audio stream (the response of the sitting person) is an important stimulus that triggers the gaze movement. Neuroscience research also shows that audio signals influence eye movements. So we address the problem of forecasting the gaze fixation of the camera-wearer in unseen future frames, using a short egocentric video clip and the corresponding audio. As Fig. 1 shows, because the model can fuse the audio and visual cues it correctly predicts the future attention to the seated subject.

Many works have addressed egocentric gaze estimation, but egocentric gaze anticipation is largely understudied. Also, how to use both the visual and the audio modality for egocentric gaze modeling has not been explored yet. Existing audio-visual learning methods commonly fuse the visual and audio embeddings simultaneously in time and space. This kind of fusion is not ideal in the egocentric setting, because the camera wearer reacts to the audio stimuli and this causes a drastic change of camera viewpoint. In Fig. 1, reacting to the question and answer, the camera wearer shifts attention from the paper to the standing person and then to the sitting person. The viewpoint and scene also changed because of head movement (see the first and last frame). Also, because of the natural delay of reaction time, the audio stimulus and the gaze reaction do not happen at the same time. So to predict future gaze behavior a model needs to (1) learn the possible viewpoint and scene change driven by the audio stream over time and (2) locate the potential future gaze target in the visual space. If the two modalities are fused in time and space simultaneously, performance on these two targets may be limited because of spurious audio-visual correlations. That is why a spatial-temporal separable fusion model is a better solution for the egocentric gaze anticipation task.

To address these challenges we propose a new Contrastive Spatial-Temporal Separable (CSTS) audio-visual fusion method for egocentric gaze anticipation. We input the egocentric video frames into a video encoder and the corresponding audio spectrograms into an audio encoder. Then we build a spatial fusion module and a temporal fusion module in parallel, based on self-attention, to model the spatial and the temporal audio-visual correlation separately, which addresses exactly the demands above. The outputs of the two branches are merged by channel-wise reweighting and given to a visual decoder that predicts the future gaze target. We also propose a new strategy that applies a multi-modal contrastive loss on the reweighted representations from the fusion modules (we call it post-fusion contrastive loss) to help audio-visual correspondence learning. We show the benefits of our approach on two egocentric video datasets that capture social scenarios and everyday activities, Ego4D and Aria. Our model achieves state-of-the-art gaze anticipation performance on both datasets. Our contributions are:

- We introduce the first approach that uses visual and audio signals to model egocentric gaze behaviors.

- We propose a new CSTS model that uses a spatio-temporal separable fusion module and a post-fusion contrastive learning scheme to help audio-visual representation learning for egocentric gaze anticipation.

- We present comprehensive experiment results on the Ego4D and Aria datasets. The ablation studies show the audio modality improves F1 score by +2.5% on Ego4D and by +2.4% on Aria. The experiments also show our model outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method by +1.9% and +1.6% in F1 score on the two datasets.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
A person’s eye movements during their daily activities reflect their intentions and goals (see [1] for a representative cognitive science study). The ability to predict the future gaze targets of the camera-wearer from egocentric videos, known as egocentric gaze anticipation, is therefore a key step towards understanding and modeling cognitive processes and decision making. This capability could also enable new applications in Augmented Reality and Wearable Computing, especially in social scenarios – for example, providing memory aids for patients with cognitive impairments, or reducing the latency of content delivery in such AR systems. However, forecasting the gaze fixations of a camera-wearer using only the egocentric view (i.e., without eye tracking at testing time) is very challenging due to the complexity of egocentric scene content and the dynamic nature of gaze behaviors.

We argue that audio signals can serve as an important auxiliary cue for egocentric gaze forecasting. Consider the example in Fig. 1. In the input sequence, the camera view shifts from the paper held by the camera wearer to the standing speaker who asks a question. Then the sitting speaker on the far right answers the question, which is captured by the audio stream. In the anticipation sequence, the camera wearer’s gaze shifts towards the sitting person’s head after hearing her response. Here, the audio stream (the sitting person’s response) is an important stimulus that triggers this gaze movement. Neuroscience research also provides evidence for the influence of audio signals on eye movements [2]. Therefore, we address the problem of forecasting the gaze fixation of the camera-wearer in unseen future frames using a short egocentric video clip and corresponding audio. As shown in Fig. 1, the model’s ability to fuse the audio and visual cues enables it to correctly predict the future attention to the seated subject.

Though many works have addressed egocentric gaze estimation [3,4,5,6,7,8,9], the egocentric gaze anticipation task is largely understudied [10]. Moreover, how to leverage both the visual and the audio modality for egocentric gaze modeling has not been explored yet. Existing methods on audio-visual learning commonly [11,12,13,14,15,16,17] fuse visual and audio embeddings simultaneously in time and space. However, such a fusion mechanism is not ideal in the egocentric setting, where the camera wearer’s reaction to the audio stimuli causes a drastic change of camera viewpoint. In Fig. 1, as a reaction to the question and answer, the camera wearer shifts attention from the paper to the standing person and then to the sitting person. The viewpoint and scene have also changed because of head movement (see the first and last frame). Moreover, due to the natural delay of reaction time, the audio stimulus and the gaze reaction will not occur at the same time. Predicting future gaze behavior therefore demands a model that can (1) learn possible viewpoint and scene change driven by the audio stream over time and (2) locate the potential future gaze target in the visual space. Fusing the two modalities in time and space simultaneously may limit performance on these two targets because of spurious audio-visual correlations. Hence, a spatial-temporal separable fusion model is a better solution for the egocentric gaze anticipation task.

To address these challenges, we propose a novel Contrastive Spatial-Temporal Separable (CSTS) audio-visual fusion method for egocentric gaze anticipation. Specifically, we input the egocentric video frames and the corresponding audio spectrograms into a video encoder and an audio encoder respectively. We then develop a spatial fusion module and a temporal fusion module in parallel, based on self-attention, for modeling the spatial and temporal audio-visual correlation separately, which exactly addresses the demands above. The output representations from the two branches are merged by channel-wise reweighting and fed into a visual decoder to predict the future gaze target. We also propose a novel strategy that applies a multi-modal contrastive loss [18] to the reweighted representations from the fusion modules (referred to as post-fusion contrastive loss) to facilitate audio-visual correspondence learning. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach on two egocentric video datasets that capture social scenarios and everyday activities: Ego4D [19] and Aria [20]. The proposed model achieves state-of-the-art gaze anticipation performance on both datasets. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- We introduce the first approach that uses visual and audio signals for modeling egocentric gaze behaviors.

- We propose a novel CSTS model that leverages a spatio-temporal separable fusion module and a post-fusion contrastive learning scheme to facilitate audio-visual representation learning for egocentric gaze anticipation.

- We present comprehensive experiment results on the Ego4D [19] and Aria [20] datasets. Our ablation studies show the audio modality improves F1 score by +2.5% on Ego4D and +2.4% on Aria. The experiments also demonstrate that our model outperforms the prior state-of-the-art method by +1.9% and +1.6% in F1 score on the two datasets.
